modules.title: Capital Structure and Sources of Finance
modules.html:
Types of Capital

TermMeaning
Authorised/nominal capitalMaximum a company may raise, stated in the memorandum
Issued capitalPart of authorised capital offered to the public
Called-up capitalPart of issued capital shareholders have been asked to pay
Paid-up capitalAmount actually paid by shareholders
Circulating/working capitalFunds for day-to-day operations
Fixed capitalLong-lived assets: land, buildings, machinery
Owner's equity/capital ownedTotal assets − total liabilities

Key Formulae

$$\text{Working Capital} = \text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Employed} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Owned} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Total Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Current Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$$

Sources of Business Finance

  • Short term – bank overdraft, trade credit, factoring, commercial paper.
  • Medium term – term loans, hire purchase, leasing, equipment finance.
  • Long term – ordinary and preference shares, debentures, bonds, mortgage loans, retained earnings, venture capital, government/development bank loans.

Choice depends on cost, duration of need, security available, control implications and repayment ability.

examples.q: A firm has current assets ₦9,200,000, current liabilities ₦3,700,000 and total assets ₦28,000,000 with long-term loans of ₦7,000,000. Compute working capital, capital employed, capital owned and the current ratio.
Which source of finance suits (i) buying a delivery van (ii) paying staff salaries in a slow month?
examples.a: (i) A medium-term hire purchase or lease matches the van's life and spreads the cost; the asset itself serves as security. (ii) A bank overdraft is best – it is short term, flexible and interest is charged only on the amount actually used.

modules.title: Business Management and Organisation
modules.html:
Elements of Management (POSDCORB / Fayol)

  1. Planning – deciding objectives and how to achieve them.
  2. Organising – arranging resources and assigning duties.
  3. Staffing – recruitment, selection, training and remuneration.
  4. Directing/Leading – guiding and motivating employees.
  5. Co-ordinating – harmonising the work of departments.
  6. Controlling – measuring performance against standards and correcting deviations.
  7. Budgeting and reporting.

Principles of Management

Division of work, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain, span of control, delegation, discipline, remuneration, esprit de corps.

Departments of a Business

DepartmentMain duties
PurchasingSourcing suppliers, ordering, stock control
ProductionManufacturing, quality control, maintenance
Marketing/SalesMarket research, promotion, distribution, after-sales
Finance/AccountsRecords, budgets, payments, financial reporting
Human resourcesRecruitment, training, welfare, industrial relations
Administration/LegalCorrespondence, compliance, contracts

Organisational Structures

  • Line – direct vertical authority; simple and quick.
  • Line and staff – line managers advised by specialists.
  • Functional – authority by specialisation.
  • Matrix/committee – cross-functional project teams.

Span of control is the number of subordinates one manager can effectively supervise; a narrow span produces a tall structure, a wide span a flat one.

examples.q: A company of 240 workers uses a span of control of 6. How many first-line supervisors are needed, and what is the effect of widening the span to 12?
examples.a: At a span of 6: \( \dfrac{240}{6} = 40 \) supervisors. At 12: \( \dfrac{240}{12} = 20 \) supervisors. Widening the span halves supervisory cost and flattens the structure, but each supervisor now oversees more staff, so control and coaching may suffer.

examples.q: Explain 'unity of command' and give one consequence of breaking it.
examples.a: Each employee should receive instructions from only one superior. Where two managers give conflicting orders, the worker becomes confused, discipline breaks down, accountability is blurred and productivity falls.

modules.title: Legal Aspects of Business
modules.html:
Contract

A contract is an agreement enforceable by law. Essential elements:

  1. Offer and acceptance
  2. Consideration – something of value exchanged
  3. Intention to create legal relations
  4. Capacity – parties must be of age and sound mind
  5. Free consent – no fraud, duress, undue influence or misrepresentation
  6. Legality of object and possibility of performance

Contracts are discharged by performance, agreement, frustration, breach or operation of law. Remedies for breach: damages, specific performance, injunction, rescission and quantum meruit.

Sale of Goods

  • Condition – a vital term; breach allows rejection of the goods.
  • Warranty – a minor term; breach gives damages only.
  • Caveat emptor – ‘let the buyer beware’, now limited by implied terms of merchantable quality and fitness for purpose.
  • Nemo dat quod non habet – no one can give a better title than he has.

Agency

An agent acts on behalf of a principal to create legal relations with third parties. Created by express/implied appointment, necessity, estoppel or ratification. Duties of an agent: obey instructions, act in person, exercise care, account for money and avoid conflicts of interest. Terminated by performance, mutual agreement, revocation, death, insanity or bankruptcy.

Modern Trends and Ethics

E-commerce, mobile payment, outsourcing, franchising, corporate social responsibility, data protection (NDPC) and anti-money-laundering compliance now shape business practice. Ethical conduct – honest advertising, fair pricing, prompt tax payment and safe products – builds sustainable goodwill.

examples.q: Chika advertises a phone for ₦180,000 in a shop window. Musa insists the shop must sell at that price. Is he right?
examples.a: No. A shop display or advertisement is an invitation to treat, not an offer. Musa's willingness to pay is the offer; the shop may accept or reject it. Only on acceptance does a binding contract arise.

examples.q: A trader buys a generator described as 'brand new' but it turns out to be refurbished. State his remedy.
examples.a: The description goes to the root of the contract, so it is a condition, not a warranty. He may repudiate the contract, reject the generator and recover his money, and additionally claim damages for any loss suffered from the misdescription.

modules.title: Working capital, capital employed and business efficiency
modules.html:
Working capital, capital employed and business efficiency is a key part of Business Administration and Legal Aspects (SSS 3, Commerce). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Types of Capital Term Meaning Authorised/nominal capital Maximum a company may raise, stated in the memorandum Issued capital Part of authorised capital offered to the public Called-up capital Part of issued capital shareholders have been asked to pay Paid-up capital Amount actually paid by shareholders Circulating/working capital Funds for day-to-day operations Fixed capital Long-lived assets: land, buildings, machinery Owner's equity/capital owned Total assets − total liabilities Key Formulae $$\text{Working Capital} = \text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Employed} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Owned} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Total Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Current Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$$ Sources of Business Finance Short term – bank overdraft, trade credit, factoring, commercial paper.
  • Long term – ordinary and preference shares, debentures, bonds, mortgage loans, retained earnings, venture capital, government/development bank loans.
  • Departments of a Business Department Main duties Purchasing Sourcing suppliers, ordering, stock control Production Manufacturing, quality control, maintenance Marketing/Sales Market research, promotion, distribution, after-sales Finance/Accounts Records, budgets, payments, financial reporting Human resources Recruitment, training, welfare, industrial relations Administration/Legal Correspondence, compliance, contracts Organisational Structures Line – direct vertical authority; simple and quick.
  • Modern Trends and Ethics E-commerce, mobile payment, outsourcing, franchising, corporate social responsibility, data protection (NDPC) and anti-money-laundering compliance now shape business practice.
  • Capital employed represents long-term funds tied up in the business.

Worked example

Q: Working capital is
A: Current assets − current liabilities — It measures funds available for day-to-day operations.

Q: Capital employed equals
A: Total assets − current liabilities — Capital employed represents long-term funds tied up in the business.

examples.a: Current assets − current liabilities — It measures funds available for day-to-day operations.
Total assets − current liabilities — Capital employed represents long-term funds tied up in the business.

quiz.q: Working capital is
quiz.solution: It measures funds available for day-to-day operations.

quiz.q: Capital employed equals
quiz.solution: Capital employed represents long-term funds tied up in the business.

quiz.q: If total assets are ₦15m and total liabilities ₦6m, capital owned is
quiz.solution: Capital owned = 15m − 6m = ₦9m.

quiz.q: The maximum capital a company may raise is its
quiz.solution: Authorised (nominal) capital is stated in the memorandum of association.

quiz.q: Which is a short-term source of finance?
quiz.solution: An overdraft is repayable on demand and used for temporary shortfalls.

quiz.q: Buying a machine on instalments while using it immediately is
quiz.solution: Under hire purchase the buyer uses the asset and owns it after the final instalment.

quiz.q: The number of subordinates a manager can effectively supervise is the
quiz.solution: Span of control determines whether a structure is tall or flat.

quiz.q: Unity of command means an employee should receive orders from
quiz.solution: Multiple bosses create confusion and conflicting instructions.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an element of a valid contract?
quiz.solution: An advertisement is usually only an invitation to treat, not an essential element.

quiz.q: Breach of a condition in a sale of goods entitles the buyer to
quiz.solution: A condition goes to the root of the contract, so the buyer may repudiate it.

quiz.q: Caveat emptor means
quiz.solution: The buyer should examine goods, though implied statutory terms now protect him.

quiz.q: A person who acts on behalf of another to make contracts is a(n)
quiz.solution: An agent creates legal relations between the principal and third parties.

quiz.q: Which department handles recruitment and training?
quiz.solution: HR manages staffing, welfare and industrial relations.

quiz.q: Current assets ₦4,000,000 and current liabilities ₦2,000,000 give a current ratio of
quiz.solution: 4,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 2:1, the conventional benchmark.

quiz.q: Nemo dat quod non habet means
options: No one can give a better title than he has
quiz.solution: A seller cannot transfer ownership he does not possess.

quiz.q: Controlling as a management function involves
options: Comparing performance with standards and correcting deviations
quiz.solution: Control closes the loop between plans and actual results.

quiz.q: Legal tender refers to:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2021). Correct answer: Money backed by law.

quiz.q: Legal tender:

quiz.q: The legal rule 'Caveat Emptor' means...
options: The king can do no wrong
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Let the buyer beware.

quiz.q: Legal tender is:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2025). Correct answer: Money backed by law.

quiz.q: The legal document for partnership is?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Partnership Deed.

quiz.q: Working Capital:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: $$ CA - CL $$.

quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2025). Correct answer: $$ CA - CL $$.

quiz.q: A specialized retailer that sells only one line of goods is a _____.
quiz.solution: A specialty shop focuses on a specific category of products, such as a pharmacy or a boutique.

quiz.q: A warehouse owned and operated by the government to store goods until duties are paid is a _____.
quiz.solution: Bonded warehouses are used to secure dutiable goods; importers cannot remove them until the customs duties are settled.

quiz.q: A document sent by a seller to a buyer when goods are delivered as a summary of the transaction is a/an _____.
quiz.solution: The invoice is a bill that gives details of the goods sold, their prices, and the total amount due.

quiz.q: A contract that is binding on only one party is described as _____.
quiz.solution: A voidable contract is one that can be affirmed or rejected by one of the parties, often due to misrepresentation or duress.

quiz.q: The document showing the evidence of a contract of insurance is the _____.
quiz.solution: The insurance policy is the formal document containing all the terms and conditions of the insurance contract.

quiz.q: The cost of transporting goods to the buyer's premises is known as _____.
quiz.solution: Carriage outward is the shipping cost paid by the seller to deliver goods to a customer.

quiz.q: A warehouse built near a port to store goods for a short time before they are loaded onto a ship is a _____.
quiz.solution: Transit sheds are temporary storage facilities at ports for goods awaiting shipment or collection.

quiz.q: A person who buys goods from a manufacturer in large quantities is a _____.
quiz.solution: Wholesalers are the middlemen who bridge the gap between large-scale producers and small-scale retailers.

quiz.q: The use of the internet to buy and sell goods and services is _____.
quiz.solution: Electronic commerce includes online shopping, digital payments, and internet banking.

quiz.q: The 'Law of Contract' requires that for an agreement to be valid, there must be _____.
quiz.solution: Offer and acceptance are the two most fundamental elements of a valid contract.

quiz.q: The practice of protecting local industries by placing high taxes on imported goods is _____.
quiz.solution: Protectionism uses tariffs and quotas to make foreign goods more expensive, encouraging people to buy local products.

quiz.q: The document issued by a seller to a buyer when goods are returned is a _____.
quiz.solution: A credit note is issued to inform the buyer that their account has been credited for returned or overcharged goods.

quiz.q: An 'unpaid seller' has the right of _____ which allows him to keep the goods until the price is paid.
quiz.solution: A lien is a legal right to keep possession of property belonging to another person until a debt owed by that person is discharged.

quiz.q: The physical path over which goods are transported by sea is governed by a document called a _____.
quiz.solution: The Bill of Lading is a document of title and a contract of carriage for goods shipped by sea.

quiz.q: Which agency in Nigeria is responsible for the standard and quality of food and drugs?
quiz.solution: The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) regulates and controls the manufacture and sale of food and drugs.

quiz.q: In a contract, an 'Offer' must be followed by _____ for a valid agreement to exist.
quiz.solution: Offer and acceptance are the two primary requirements for the formation of a binding contract.

quiz.q: Which of the following allows a trader to buy goods now and pay at a future date?
quiz.solution: Credit trade enables business expansion by allowing buyers to manage their cash flow.

quiz.q: A contract that is not legally enforceable from the beginning is _____.
quiz.solution: A void contract has no legal effect and cannot be enforced by either party.

quiz.q: Which document shows the details of goods sent?
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2021). Correct answer: Invoice.

quiz.q: A Valid Contract must have:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2021). Correct answer: Offer and Acceptance.

quiz.q: The document that shows the details of goods sent by a supplier to a buyer is:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2022). Correct answer: Invoice.

quiz.q: The portion of authorized capital that has been issued to shareholders is:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2022). Correct answer: Issued capital.

quiz.q: Capital of a PLC is divided into:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: Shares.

quiz.q: The process of making goods available to the final consumer is known as...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Distribution.

quiz.q: The document that regulates the internal management of a company is the...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Articles of Association.

quiz.q: The government agency responsible for ensuring the quality of food and drugs in Nigeria is...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: NAFDAC.

quiz.q: A contract is a legally binding...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Agreement.
